# Relative container volume inside the actual projection

Let `P=pi(C)` be the actual integer-coordinate projection of a convex body.
This note studies containers `L` with `K subset L subset P`, where
`K=pi(D_alpha)` is a nonempty compact depth-region projection. The finite
volume optimization now attains its maximum, but its variation identities
contain boundary forces from `P`. Those forces cannot be discarded as
carrying zero mixed-integer mass.

## 1. Attainment with a fixed finite set of cut directions

Let `P subset R^n` be a convex body, `K` a nonempty compact subset of `P`,
and `a_1,...,a_N` fixed unit vectors. Put

    L(b)=P intersect intersection_i {z:a_i.z<=b_i}.

It suffices to take offsets in the compact box

    h_K(a_i)<=b_i<=h_P(a_i).                         (1)

Offsets larger than the upper endpoint define a redundant cut; the lower
endpoint is exactly the containment requirement. Define feasibility by

    int(L(b)) intersect Z^n=empty.                   (2)

Assuming there is a feasible parameter, a maximum of ordinary `n`-volume
is attained in this class. No full-dimensionality of `K` is required.

Proof. The feasible parameter set is closed. If `b^(k)->b` and an integer
point `p` were interior to `L(b)`, then `p` would be interior to `P` and
would strictly satisfy all the finitely many cut inequalities. Those
strict inequalities persist for large `k`, putting `p` in the interior
of `L(b^(k))`, a contradiction.

The volume is upper semicontinuous, which is enough for maximization.
For any `epsilon>0`, one has eventually
`L(b^(k)) subset L(b)+epsilon B_n`. Otherwise points violating this
inclusion have a convergent subsequence in compact `P`, whose limit
satisfies every limiting cut and hence lies in `L(b)`. Thus

    limsup_k |L(b^(k))| <= |L(b)+epsilon B_n|.

As `epsilon` decreases to zero, measure continuity from above gives
the required upper bound by `|L(b)|`, including when the limiting
intersection is lower dimensional. Compactness of (1) proves attainment.

This proves attainment for INTERIOR lattice exclusion. Requiring that
`L` contain no lattice point even on its boundary need not give a closed
class and need not attain its volume supremum; Section 5 gives an exact
example inside the actual projection.

## 2. Relative offset maximality and its lattice contacts

Suppose the attained maximum has positive volume. Remove redundant cuts
and merge identical copies when discussing its actual new facets. A new
facet means a facet on a moving cut plane whose relative interior lies
in `int(P)`, rather than a piece inherited from `boundary P`. Write

    F_i=L intersect {a_i.z=b_i},
    A_i=H_(n-1)(F_i)>0,
    c_i=the centroid of F_i.

Intersections with other facets or with `boundary P` have zero facet
measure here. Every such new facet at an offset maximum contains a point

    p_i in relint(F_i) intersect int(P) intersect Z^n.              (3)

Proof. Increasing only `b_i` preserves `K subset L subset P`. Its volume
derivative is `A_i>0`, by integrating the outward prism over the facet.
An integer point initially on another moving facet stays out of the
interior because that inequality is unchanged. An integer point on
`boundary P` also stays out of the interior, regardless of the moving
cut. Every other initially excluded integer point has a positive gap in
one of the finitely many inequalities; there are only finitely many
integer points in `P`. If no point in (3) existed, all these exclusions
would therefore persist under a sufficiently small positive offset
increase, contradicting maximality.

Consequently `b_i=a_i.p_i`. This contact identity is valid with fixed
normals. A facet-CENTROID identity is stronger and does not follow from
offset variations alone: arbitrary normal rotations may cut `K` or lie
outside the specified finite directional family.

For the actual projection `P=pi(C)`, an integer witness in `int(P)` has a
full-dimensional continuous fiber. To see this, take an interior ball of
`C` centered above some `z_c`. Extend the segment from `z_c` through the
witness slightly past it to a point `w in P`, and choose any point of
`C_w`. The witness lies at a convex-combination parameter strictly less
than one on this segment. Combining the chosen point with the interior
ball leaves a positive-radius continuous ball in the witness fiber.
If the witness equals `z_c`, the original ball suffices. Thus interior
contacts correspond to positive full mixed-volume fibers; boundary
contacts need separate treatment.
In particular, a nonempty intersection with intrinsic dimension `q<d`
forces `int(P) intersect Z^n=empty`, since an interior integer index
would give a `d`-dimensional fiber. Its positive intrinsic mass therefore
lies entirely over the projection boundary.

## 3. Exact outer-boundary terms

Let `Gamma_P` be the portion of `boundary L` inherited from `boundary P`,
and let `n_P(z)` be its outward unit normal, defined almost everywhere.
For a polytope, the following integrals are simply finite sums over its
inherited facets. For a general convex body they use the ordinary
Gauss--Green formula on its Lipschitz boundary. Let `q in int(L)`.
The point `q` is only a reference for the divergence identity; it is not
being proposed as a mixed-integer center.
Decomposing the boundary gives the exact identities

    sum_i A_i a_i + integral_(Gamma_P) n_P(z) dH_(n-1)(z)=0,        (4)

    sum_i A_i a_i(c_i-q)^T
      + integral_(Gamma_P) n_P(z)(z-q)^T dH_(n-1)(z)
      = |L| I_n.                                                  (5)

Taking the trace yields

    n|L|=sum_i A_i(b_i-a_i.q)+Phi_P(q),                            (6)
    Phi_P(q)=integral_(Gamma_P) (z-q).n_P(z) dH_(n-1)(z).

The coefficient is exactly `n`. At an offset maximum, (3) gives

    n|L|=sum_i A_i a_i.(p_i-q)+Phi_P(q).                           (7)

All terms in the scalar identity are nonnegative: the cut support
distances are positive at `q`, and a supporting plane of convex `P`
has `(z-q).n_P(z)>=dist(q,boundary P)>0`. In particular `Phi_P(q)>0`
whenever the inherited boundary has positive surface measure.

Equation (7), rather than its version with `Phi_P` removed, is the
relative contact identity. The centroid `c_i` in (5) cannot be replaced
by the arbitrary integer witness `p_i` from an offset variation.

Here is a direct admissible-template deformation calculation. Move only
the free cut planes homothetically away from `q`, keeping `P` fixed:

    b_i(t)=b_i+t(b_i-a_i.q).

At proper new facets its ordinary volume derivative is

    d|L(b(t))|/dt at t=0
       =sum_i A_i(b_i-a_i.q)=n|L|-Phi_P(q).                         (8)

This is not a homothety of the whole container; its inherited `P`
boundary stays fixed. The outward direction preserves containment of
`K`, but at an offset maximum with a new facet it is not lattice-feasible:
the witness (3) would enter the interior.

For completeness, if rotations of the free planes are separately
authorized, an affine physical motion `z -> z+t(Bz+v)` of their defining
intersection, followed by clipping to the fixed `P`, has first derivative

    sum_i A_i a_i.(B c_i+v)
      =|L| tr(B)-integral_(Gamma_P) n_P(z).(Bz+v) dH_(n-1)(z).      (9)

This follows by the facet normal velocity and (4)--(5). It is an identity
for that specified deformation, not a claim that rotations are allowed
in the fixed-normal optimization class. Positive-area coincidences with
`P` facets are assigned to the inherited boundary; attempting to move a
coincident redundant cut inward instead creates a one-sided prism and
requires its separate, nonsmooth trace. No coincident owner is silently
counted twice in (4)--(9).

## 4. Which outer normals carry mixed-integer mass?

Return to the actual convex body `C` and its mixed measure `mu`, without
normalizing the total mass. For a nonzero base normal `v`, let

    h=h_P(v),   E_P(v)={z in P:v.z=h}.

The CLOSED vertical support cap has exactly the mass

    mu({(z,x):v.z>=h})
      =sum_(z in E_P(v) intersect Z^n) mu_z(C_z).                  (10)

Every included fiber is included in full. Formula (10) is just the
finite fiber sum and remains valid for the intrinsic Hausdorff measure,
with its own positive-measure fibers. The strict exterior cap `v.z>h`
has mass zero. These two caps are not interchangeable.

There is an exact jump, not an infinitesimal continuous loss. If the
finite set of integer fibers outside `E_P(v)` is nonempty, let

    delta=min{h-v.z:z in pi(S), v.z<h}>0.

For `0<epsilon<delta`, the cap with threshold `h-epsilon` has exactly
the mass in (10), while the cap with threshold `h+epsilon` has mass
zero. At threshold `h`, the closed cap retains all of (10). If there are
no outside fibers, the same assertion holds for every sufficiently small
positive epsilon. Thus even a zero-area set of base boundary indices can
carry all relevant fiber measure. The ordinary boundary integrals in
(4)--(9) do not turn this jump into a zero mixed-volume term.

## 5. A fully explicit attained example with all mass on the outer boundary

Use the actual product from
`candidate 75212e124d66e084`:

    C=[0,1]^2 x [-1,1],
    S={0,1}^2 x [-1,1],   M=8,
    alpha=1/5,  K=pi(D_alpha).

That note proves that `D_alpha` is full dimensional, avoids the mixed
lattice, and that `K` lies in the rational corner-truncated octagon

    P_0={z in [0,1]^2:q_v(z)>=3/10 for every binary vertex v}.

Here `q_v(z)=sum_j[(1-v_j)z_j+v_j(1-z_j)]` is the globally affine
extension of the distance formula on the unit square. Its sublevel sets
in the cap statements below are actual ambient halfspaces.

Take the actual projection `P=[0,1]^2` and the fixed four corner-cut
directions. Write the cuts as `q_v(z)>=epsilon_v`, with admissible
offsets containing `K`. The parameter choice `epsilon_v=0` gives `L=P`.
It is interior lattice-free, so it is feasible and is the unique
maximum-volume container in this class. Its area is `1`.

More generally this conclusion is automatic whenever the actual
projection is HOLLOW, meaning `int(P) intersect Z^n=empty`: the parameter
choice `b_i=h_P(a_i)` gives the feasible container `L=P`, which plainly
maximizes volume over every relative container. Thus in hollow
projections the relative volume optimum is independent of the fiber
bodies and of `K`. It adds no new restriction on those fibers.

At the cube optimum, there are no genuine new facets. With
`q=(1/2,1/2)`, each of the four inherited edges has length `1` and
support distance `1/2`. Therefore

    Phi_P(q)=4(1)(1/2)=2=n|P|.                                    (11)

The matrix integral in (5) is `I_2`, and the vector integral in (4) is
zero. Every scalar contribution in (11) is strictly positive. Meanwhile
ALL eight units of mixed-integer length lie on the boundary of `P`.
For each coordinate facet, the closed vertical support cap contains two
whole interval fibers and has mass `4=M/2`.

In particular that outer-facet mass is not bounded by the total budget
of one group of `d+1=2` bad caps at this depth threshold:

    4 > (d+1)alpha M = 16/5.

Thus these full boundary layers cannot automatically be charged to one
two-cap group of masses below `alpha M`. This is a concrete failure of
that proposed use of the existing cap budget; it is not an OC
counterexample, whose required constant here is `1/8`.

The limiting behavior is equally explicit. For `0<epsilon<=3/10`, set

    L_epsilon=P intersect {q_v(z)>=epsilon for all four v}.

It contains `K`, avoids all integer points even on its boundary, and

    |L_epsilon|=1-2epsilon^2 -> 1.

The inherited part of each coordinate edge has length `1-2epsilon`, so

    Phi_P(q)=2-4epsilon.

Each of the four new corner facets has length `sqrt(2)epsilon` and
support distance `(1-epsilon)/sqrt(2)` from `q`. Thus (6) reads exactly

    2(1-2epsilon^2)
      =4epsilon(1-epsilon)+(2-4epsilon).                           (12)

Despite Hausdorff convergence and the quadratic loss of ordinary area,

    mu(S intersect (L_epsilon x R))=0  for every epsilon>0,
    mu(S intersect (P x R))=8.

All four binary base points are removed by their own corner cuts. Each
open exterior corner cap `q_v(z)<epsilon` contains one full interval
fiber and has mass `2`, although its projection area is only
`epsilon^2/2`. Its normalized mass `1/4` exceeds `alpha=1/5`.

This also proves nonattainment in the CLOSED-lattice-exclusion relative
class. Its area supremum is `1`, approached by the `L_epsilon`, but only
`P` has that area among closed convex subsets of `P`, and `P` contains
four boundary lattice points.

## Scope

Using the actual projection supplies genuine compactness and the exact
relative identity (7). It does not remove outer forces: in the hollow
case they can supply the entire volume identity while the boundary
fibers supply the entire mixed-integer measure. A quantitative closing
argument would need additional cap information controlling these actual
boundary-fiber terms; neither zero ordinary boundary volume nor the
attained relative-container maximum provides such control.
